spans.note: statement of the hypothesis being tested

spans.assertion: the hypothesis is judged supported by the data
very dark-skinned players have an adjusted probability of receiving a red card 0.295 percentage points higher (95% CI [0.063,0.526]) than very light-skinned players
the adjusted odds ratio for very dark vs very light players is 1.280 (95% CI [1.035,1.582], two-sided p=0.023, α=0.05)
the point estimate for the adjusted risk difference is 0.295 percentage points
the 95% CI for the adjusted risk difference is [0.063, 0.526] pp
the two-sided p-value for the adjusted risk difference is 0.023 against α=0.05
the risk difference was adjusted for games played, yellow cards, player position, height, weight, league country, and referee country implicit bias
given a baseline red card rate of ~1.1% for very light-skinned players, the effect represents a relative increase of approximately 27%
the point estimate for the adjusted odds ratio is 1.280
the 95% CI for the adjusted odds ratio is [1.035, 1.582]
dark-skinned players have 28% higher odds of receiving a red card than light-skinned players after covariate adjustment
the lower CI bound of 1.035 indicates the effect is statistically distinguishable from the null at α=0.05 two-sided
the unit of analysis was defined as player-referee dyads
the primary analysis used 62,010 dyads involving 783 unique players (extreme groups)
the complete dataset comprised 124,621 dyads involving 1,585 unique players with skin tone ratings
the primary specification used an extreme-groups comparison to maximize signal detection
very dark was defined as skin tone > 0.75 (N=10,411 dyads)
very light was defined as skin tone < 0.25 (N=51,599 dyads)
skin tone was coded by two independent raters on a 0-1 scale
inter-rater reliability between the two skin-tone raters was high (r=0.923)
the average of the two raters' ratings was used as the skin tone score
extreme-groups dichotomization was chosen because it is theoretically motivated and maximizes statistical power by focusing on the ends of the distribution
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for any red card received in the dyad
the overall red card rate was 1.26% of dyads
continuous covariates (standardized) included games played, yellow cards received, height, weight, and mean referee-country IAT score
categorical covariates included player position (12 categories) and league country (England, Germany, France, Spain)
missing height (N=46) and weight (N=753) were imputed with the standardized median (0), treated as a standard approach for small proportions of missing continuous covariates
a logistic regression model was fit via maximum likelihood estimation
the risk difference was computed via g-computation (marginal standardization), predicting outcomes for all observations under each exposure level and averaging the difference
standard errors were model-based (Wald)
standard errors did not account for clustering by player, despite clustering by player being appropriate since the same player appears in multiple dyads
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings due to unavailable player photos, treated as complete-case analysis
no other exclusions were applied; all dyads with skin tone ratings were retained
continuous covariates were standardized (mean 0, SD 1) for numerical stability
skin tone was dichotomized into extreme groups for the primary analysis
skin tone was also analyzed as a continuous variable in sensitivity analyses
the primary analysis was repeated under four alternative specifications
all four alternative specifications showed positive effects in the hypothesized direction with significance at α=0.05

spans.assertion: primary extreme-groups specification: N=62,010, adjusted OR=1.280 [1.035,1.582], adjusted RD=0.295pp, p=0.023
dark>0.625 (full sample) specification: N=124,621, OR=1.180 [1.012,1.375], RD=0.211pp, p=0.034
continuous (75th vs 25th percentile) specification: N=124,621, OR=1.098 [1.022,1.178], RD=0.110pp, p=0.010
exclude-goalkeepers specification: N=113,568, OR=1.178 [1.008,1.377], RD=0.209pp, p=0.039
without-yellow-cards-control specification: N=124,621, OR=1.173 [1.007,1.367], RD=0.204pp, p=0.041
the extreme-groups specification yields the largest effect (0.295pp), as expected given the contrast between darkest and lightest players
alternative cutpoints (>0.625) and continuous coding yield smaller but still significant effects (0.11-0.21pp)
excluding goalkeepers does not materially change results
controlling for yellow cards slightly attenuates but does not eliminate the effect
the attenuation-but-persistence pattern is interpreted as suggesting both direct and indirect (mediated) pathways of bias
all specifications are statistically significant at α=0.05, taken to demonstrate robustness

an exploratory interaction between skin tone and referee-country implicit bias was tested and found non-significant (p=0.47), interpreted as the skin-tone effect not varying strongly by referee-country bias level
based on the magnitude, precision, and direction of the primary estimand, the hypothesis is judged SUPPORTED
the adjusted RD of 0.295pp is characterized as a meaningful increase, ~27% relative to the baseline rate of 1.1%
the 95% CI excludes zero and the p-value (0.023) is below the 0.05 threshold, cited as evidence of precision
all specifications show positive effects (dark>light), consistent with the hypothesis
the finding is characterized as robust across multiple operationalizations of skin tone, covariate sets, and sample restrictions
after adjustment, very dark-skinned players are concluded to face a higher probability of red cards than very light-skinned players, consistent with referee bias based on skin tone
the two raters' skin tone assessments were averaged, justified by high inter-rater reliability (r=0.923)
excluding 14.7% of dyads with missing skin tone is treated as defensible since no photo was available for rating
further exploration of whether missingness in skin tone relates to outcomes was not performed, deemed beyond the scope of this exploratory analysis
standardizing covariates is described as standard practice for logistic regression to improve numerical stability and interpretability

extreme groups was used as the primary specification because it is theoretically motivated, maximizes signal, and is a common exploratory approach for establishing an effect before dose-response analysis
multiple cutpoints (0.5, 0.625, 0.75) and continuous coding were explored
the primary extreme-groups specification yielded the strongest effect, described as expected
covariates were selected a priori based on domain knowledge, each treated as a plausible confounder
model-based (Wald) standard errors were used, described as standard for logistic regression
player-level clustering was not implemented because it was computationally challenging with the software tools used, even though it would have been more conservative
the reported standard errors are judged likely anti-conservative (too small), meaning p-values may be slightly too small and CIs too narrow
the lack of clustering is stated as a limitation that would be addressed in future confirmatory work
two-sided p-values were reported throughout, per the user's request
a one-sided test, consistent with the directional hypothesis, would yield p/2, further strengthening the evidence
